DMAR

DMAR (Design, Measurement, and Analysis in R, pronounced “Dee-Mar”) is a package for human-centered research: effect sizes, confidence intervals for effect sizes, sample size planning, reliability and agreement, mediation analysis (from the simple mediation model to likelihood ratio tests of arbitrary indirect effects, with moderated mediation probing), equivalence testing, meta-analysis, experimental and quasi-experimental designs, repeated measures, and model comparison-based inference. It draws on the psychometric and statistical traditions and reflects the methodological and applied research program of its author, Ken Kelley (University of Notre Dame). It aims to be methodologically sound and useful across psychology, sociology, education, management, marketing, and information systems, especially where the independent or dependent variables involve the person.

Installation 

# The released version, from CRAN:
install.packages("DMAR")

# The development version, from GitHub:
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("yelleKneK/DMAR")

Each CRAN release is tagged on GitHub (v1.0.0 for the first); between releases the GitHub copy carries the changes of the next one, listed in NEWS.

R >= 4.0.0 is required. Most estimation, inference, and planning functions return a tidy data.frame(term, value) that composes naturally with dplyr / ggplot2 pipelines and with broom::tidy() / broom::glance(). Heavier dependencies (e.g., lavaan, lme4, OpenMx) are in Suggests and gated by requireNamespace(); install them only when you need the functions that use them.

Function Families

DMAR is organized into these function families:

  • Effect size estimates. smd(), cles(), proportion_of_superiority() (sometimes called Cohen’s U3), cliff_delta(), vargha_delaney_A(), cohen_f(), eta_squared(), omega_squared(), nnt_from_smd().
  • Confidence intervals for effect sizes. ci_smd(), ci_R2(), ci_eta_squared(), ci_omega_squared(), ci_rmsea(), ci_cv(), ci_c(), ci_sc(), ci_c_ancova(), ci_sc_ancova(), ci_reg_coef(), ci_eigenvalue(), ci_mahalanobis(), ci_ratio_of_means() and ci_ratio_of_means_paired() (Fieller’s set), ci_proportion_paired() (two proportions on the same units), ci_crossed() (units crossed with raters), and ci_two_phase() (a costly measurement with an inexpensive proxy).
  • Sample size planning under AIPE (accuracy in parameter estimation). The ss_aipe_*() family covers SMD, R², ω², CV, partial / semipartial r, regression coefficients (standardized and unstandardized), ANCOVA contrasts, RMSEA, SEM paths, polynomial change, mixed-effects fixed effects, ICC, reliability, Cliff’s delta, a single mean (ss_aipe_mean()), crossed designs of units and raters (ss_aipe_crossed()), and two-phase sampling (ss_aipe_two_phase(), ss_aipe_two_phase_cost()). Most planners have a Monte Carlo *_sensitivity() sibling that quantifies the impact of misspecified planning values; ss_aipe_two_phase_sensitivity() also evaluates the designs of ss_aipe_two_phase_cost().
  • Sample size planning under power. ss_power_R2(), ss_power_R2_change(), ss_power_smd(), ss_power_r(), ss_power_one_way_anova(), ss_power_factorial_anova(), ss_power_rm_anova(), ss_power_split_plot_anova(), ss_power_mixed_effects(), ss_power_pcm(), ss_power_sem(), ss_power_contrast(), power_fisher_exact().
  • Minimum risk / sequential estimation. mr_smd(), mr_cv(), ss_seq_c() (with ss_seq_c_sensitivity()), and ss_seq_two_phase() (a mean under two-phase sampling).
  • Equivalence testing. equivalence_smd(), equivalence_r(), equivalence_c() (with nonsuperiority), equivalence_rmsea(), equivalence_proportion_paired(), ss_aipe_equivalence_smd().
  • Reliability. reliability_alpha(), reliability_omega(), reliability_omega_categorical(), reliability_H(), reliability_kr20(), bifactor_indices() and ci_bifactor_indices() (omega hierarchical and its relatives), var_alpha(), the umbrella reliability(), and ss_aipe_reliability().
  • Factor analysis and structural equation models. fa_confirmatory() (with cfa_1() and cfa_2()), fa_exploratory() (including target rotation), factor_count(), parallel_analysis(), fa_bifactor(), fa_second_order(), factor_scores(), factor_congruence(), measurement_invariance(), sem_fit_measures(), sem_residual_fit(), sem_information_criteria(), sem_exact_fit_bootstrap(), compare_sem(), sem_sam(), htmt(), and the common method variance procedures (common_method_marker(), common_method_adjusted_r(), common_method_single_factor()).
  • Missing data. Full information maximum likelihood (the default for continuous items in the factor analysis functions and in reliability_alpha(), reliability_omega(), and reliability_H()) and two-stage maximum likelihood (in fa_confirmatory(), cfa_1(), cfa_2(), measurement_invariance(), reliability_alpha(), and reliability_omega()), with fraction_missing_information(), missing_patterns(), missing_coverage(), cov_fiml(), df_missing(), and df_barnard_rubin() for what the missing values cost.
  • ANOVA / ANCOVA / contrasts. welch_t(), contrast_test(), summary_t_test(), ancova(), mixed_anova(), manova_split_plot(), anova_within(), anova_within_two_way(), pairwise_within(), simple_effects_AB(), obrien_test(), mauchly_test(), epsilon_corrections(), contrast_adjusted().
  • Multiple-comparison procedures. ci_dunnett(), ci_tukey_kramer(), ci_games_howell(), ci_dunnett_t3(), ci_scheffe(), and their critical-value helpers cv_dunnett(), cv_smm(), cv_scheffe(), cv_tukey_hsd(), cv_t(), cv_z().
  • Agreement and reliability of raters. icc(), icc_lmer(), cohen_kappa(), fleiss_kappa(), gwet_ac(), krippendorff_alpha(), lin_ccc(), limits_of_agreement().
  • Multilevel and multivariate methods. mlmr(), mlmr_mv(), R2_mixed_effects(), R2_mixed_effects_decomposition(), compare_cov_structures(), covmat_from_cfa(), cov_sem(), procrustes_phi().
  • Longitudinal designs. ss_aipe_pcm(), ss_power_pcm(), plot_trajectories(), plot_trajectories_fitted(), variance_components_mls().
  • Design utilities. design_effect() (Kish’s design effect and DEFT), effects_coding(), helmert_coding(), is_orthogonal_set(), simulate_anova_data(), simulate_ancova_data(), simulate_regression_data().
  • Parameterization conversions (convert_*). Invertible maps between equivalent metrics (convert_r_Z / convert_Z_r, convert_R2_f / convert_f_R2, convert_lambda_R2 / convert_R2_lambda, convert_delta_lambda / convert_lambda_delta, convert_d_r / convert_r_d, convert_d_or / convert_or_d, convert_F_chisq / convert_chisq_F, convert_cor_cov).
  • Plots. plot_smd(), plot_ci(), and plot_R2() show an effect size with its CI and, given the sample sizes, the sample size; plot_trajectories() and plot_trajectories_fitted() show observed and fitted individual trajectories.
  • Variance utilities. var_smd(), var_R2(), var_r(), var_partial_r(), var_semipartial_r(), var_cv(), var_omega_squared(), var_alpha(), var_icc(), var_indirect_effect().

Canonical Examples

1. Standardized Mean Difference With a Noncentral t Confidence Interval 

library(DMAR)

# From summary statistics:
smd(mean_1 = 60, mean_2 = 55, s_1 = 10, s_2 = 10, n_1 = 30, n_2 = 30)
term value
smd 0.500 

# CI on the standardized mean difference (Cohen's d) via the noncentral t:
ci_smd(smd = 0.5, n_1 = 30, n_2 = 30, conf_level = 0.95)
term value
ci_lower -0.016
smd 0.500
ci_upper 1.012

Confidence level: 95%

2. R² With a Noncentral F Confidence Interval and AIPE Sample Size 

ci_R2(R2 = 0.30, N = 100, p = 4, conf_level = 0.95)
term value prob_less prob_greater
ci_lower 0.130 0.025 0.975
R2 0.300 NA NA
ci_upper 0.430 0.975 0.025

Confidence level: 95%


# What N is needed so the 95% CI on R^2 has full width <= 0.20?
ss_aipe_R2(true_R2 = 0.30, width = 0.20, p = 4)
term value
necessary_N 228

Confidence level: 95%

3. AIPE Planning With a Sensitivity Check 

# Plan N for a half-width of .10 on the SMD at a population SMD of 0.40.
ss_aipe_smd(true_smd = 0.40, width = 0.20)
term value
necessary_n_per_group 784
true_smd 0.400
width 0.200

Confidence level: 95%


# How does that plan hold up if the population SMD is actually 0.25?
set.seed(113)
ss_aipe_smd_sensitivity(
  true_smd      = 0.25,
  supposed_smd  = 0.40,
  width         = 0.20,
  G               = 200,

5. Reliability With a Confidence Interval 

# Cronbach's alpha plus the Bonett (2002) CI from a covariance matrix.
S <- matrix(
  c(1.0, 0.6, 0.5, 0.5,
    0.6, 1.0, 0.6, 0.5,
    0.5, 0.6, 1.0, 0.6,
    0.5, 0.5, 0.6, 1.0),
  nrow = 4)
reliability_alpha(S = S, N = 250, ci_method = "bonett")

conf_level 0.950

           22, 25, 26, 28, 28, 30, 30, 30, 30, 30)

Numerical Validation

DMAR ships a dedicated numerical-correctness test suite (tests/testthat/test-numerical-correctness.R and companion files) that pins its output against authoritative reference implementations and published values, so results are reproducible and checkable:

Quantity Reference Agreement
Confidence intervals for R², SMD; noncentral t / F limits; AIPE sample sizes MBESS 1e-5 to 1e-6 (integer N)
Within-subjects sphericity epsilons; factorial ANOVA / ANCOVA car machine precision
CFA, coefficient omega, RMSEA lavaan, semTools machine precision
krippendorff_alpha(), gwet_ac() irr, irrCAC machine precision (validated designs)
R2_mixed_effects() (Nakagawa & Schielzeth), R2_mixed_effects_decomposition() (Rights & Sterba) r2mlm machine precision (validated model classes)
Multiple-comparison critical values and CIs multcomp, published tables published values
Dunnett’s T3; the paired-proportion score interval; Fieller’s ratio of means; bifactor and second-order omegas PMCMRplus, PropCIs, mratios, semTools pinned values, compared live by the maintainer’s release tooling

The machine-precision rows hold for the model and design classes the test suite pins, including the boundary cases the tests cover. The mixed-effects R-squared functions match r2mlm and the direct Johnson quadratic form across random-intercept, correlated random-slope, split (||) random-slope, multi-slope, and nested two-level models; on split random-slope models performance/insight omits the random-slope variance, so DMAR agrees with r2mlm and the Johnson form there and not with performance. The agreement procedures match irr and irrCAC on the ordinary rating designs and on the boundary cases the tests cover: the zero-distance case of ratio-metric Krippendorff’s alpha, all-missing units in gwet_ac(), and incomplete category sets in cohen_kappa().

Relation to MBESS

DMAR is a more general and greatly expanded reimagining of the MBESS package (Kelley, 2007a, Journal of Statistical Software, 20(8), 1–24; 2007b, Behavior Research Methods, 39(4), 979–984), which has been on CRAN for about two decades. MBESS was named for the behavioral, educational, and social sciences, but the methods it implements apply across the empirical sciences, and DMAR is framed for that broader range. The notational and programming changes (uniform snake_case, tidy data.frame(term, value) returns, native ggplot2 plotting, broader coverage of within-subjects, multivariate, mixed-effects, and sequential-estimation methods) were too extensive to ship under the MBESS name without breaking compatibility, so the work ships under a new name. MBESS remains on CRAN, and new methods are added to DMAR. See vignette("mbess_to_dmar") for the MBESS → DMAR migration mapping.

Relation to Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley (MDK, 4th ed.)

Many of the methods in DMAR are discussed in Maxwell, Delaney, and Kelley (2027), Designing Experiments and Analyzing Data: A Model Comparison Perspective (4th ed., Routledge). Functions cite the specific MDK chapter in their @references block where the underlying method is discussed in detail. DMAR is broader than MDK: it covers methods (e.g., minimum risk sequential estimation, equivalence testing, mediation effect size CIs, design effects for cluster sampling) that are outside the scope of a textbook on experimental design. Conversely, MDK covers conceptual material that falls outside the scope of an R package. The two are complementary.

Related Packages

BUCSS (Bias and Uncertainty Corrected Sample Size; Kelley, Anderson, and Maxwell) plans the sample size of a future study for statistical power from the summary statistics of a prior study, correcting the prior study’s effect for publication bias and for uncertainty. Ken Kelley is a coauthor of BUCSS. Its planners cover many of the designs of DMAR’s ss_power_*() family; DMAR’s power planners take the planning effect as given, and DMAR’s ss_aipe_*() planners plan for the width of a confidence interval rather than for power.

Citation

If you use DMAR in published work, please cite

Kelley, K. (2026). DMAR: Design, Measurement, and Analysis in R. R package version 1.1.0. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22960335

and, where appropriate, the original MBESS references for the methodological lineage:

Kelley, K. (2007). Confidence Intervals for Standardized Effect Sizes: Theory, Application, and Implementation. Journal of Statistical Software, 20(8), 1–24. doi:10.18637/jss.v020.i08

Kelley, K. (2007). Methods for the Behavioral, Educational, and Social Sciences: An R package. Behavior Research Methods, 39(4), 979–984. doi:10.3758/BF03192993

Feedback

Bug reports, feature requests, and suggestions for new methods are welcomed by email to Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu (please put “DMAR” in the subject line). See https://kenkelley.org and https://kenkelley.org/publications/ for related publications.
